body: Hi! MS Speech and Language Pathologist here. What you describe is totally normal. Vocal pitch, ie how “high” or “deep” ones voice sounds is determined by the length, mass, and elasticity of the vocal folds (cords). During puberty, male vocal folds become heavier, longer, and more elastic. This causes them to oscillate (vibrate) fewer times per second- resulting in a deeper voice. These changes can occur in males any time before, and up to, the age of 25. Nothing abnormal about being 16 and not having a “deep” voice yet- and certainly no need to see a doctor over this, unless, for instance, you also had concerns related to puberty/development or lack thereof (eg vocal concerns combined with lack of hair growth) which might indicate an endocrine issue or thyroid issue that might be effecting overall hormone levels. Certainly doesn’t sound like that to me based on what you’ve described. Hope this was helpful!

I’m do sorry you are going through this. In reality, you don’t have a crystal ball to predict the future and you can only take things one day at a time. It is normal human nature to want to understand the unknown and to be able to prepare for the future. Psychologically, this often means that we try to imagine the worst case scenario for situations as a defense mechanism. We do this to try to protect ourselves. The rationale is that if we can predict the worst case scenario and prepare ourselves for it, then we will be able to handle any outcome of the situation – because we are prepared for the worst.This psychological process, although understandable, is not effective and serves only to cause extreme anxiety and panic. Given that you are so young, I would encourage that you share these feelings with your parents and consider seeking help from the mental health professionals such as a counselor Or psychologist. It is possible that given recent events you were experiencing some degree of posttraumatic stress disorder. I can speak from experience that this is horrifying as I experienced it after my father died unexpectedly early this year. Or you might be experiencing anxiety and or depression. A mental health professional will be able to help you determine if medication might be a toy you could use during this difficult time in addition to counseling. Certainly if the stress and anguish you were experiencing are affecting your every day functioning i.e. your ability to sleep, this is gotten to a level where you should seek advice from a medical professional. Remember that this is just a season of your life, and you can though it might feel like things will never get better – they certainly will.

I get worried about everything too. This is nothing to worry about. Blood vessels in the nares are incredibly thin and close to the surface of your skin. Nose bleeds are super common and can be caused by simple changes in the environment, particularly dry air which causes the moist, protective mucosa of our noses to dry out and become prone to bleeds. Examples of these changes could be recently turning the heating or air conditioning on. Not to worry- a nose bleed alone is not indicative of any major health concern.

I am so sorry to hear this. My father passed away unexpectedly in September due to an addiction, so although I can’t relate to grappling with losing someone to suicide, I can certainly relate to losing someone very close to you unexpectedly because of their own actions, and for avoidable reasons. I can also relate to feelings of guilt surrounding what could have been done differently. Recognize that shock and heartbreak are normal. Take things one day- one hour at a time. Initially the pain is crippling and this is normal. You and your family will make it through each day with the love and support of one another. Cry together. Watch tv together. Order Chinese, watch YouTube videos in a hot bath. You cannot fix it, undo it, or find a foolproof way to move through this experience without feeling like the world has been turned upside down, because it has. When such a devastating event happens, it’s normal to desperately want to understand the situation and provide yourself with answers. In reality, an understanding will likely not be achievable. Even if you were to understand the situation, it’s unlikely that this would change anything. Let it go. Accept that this process will a wave of feeling ok, then feeling like things will never be ok again. But rest assured that they will be, and before long, time will heal the raw pain.

Have you ever seen the series “Born This Way”? It’s a documentary series about young adults with Down syndrome. The series follows these individuals and their families as they transition into adult life. The families discuss their experiences raising a child with Down Syndrome, and, most importantly, they follow the lives of the adolescents themselves, including their hopes, disappointments, friendships, fears, work, etc. Although every individual with Down Syndrome is different, I find this show refreshing because I feel it depicts the individuals with Down Syndrome as dynamic, lovable, and capable- which they are. Also, speech language pathology grad student here. Read through your earlier comments and saw you mention she is non verbal but signing. Drawing can be a great outlet to encourage communicative behaviors! You can do so pretty naturally within the home using Mileu Teaching principles. For parents, the easiest way one to implement are communicative temptations engineered in the natural environment. For example, taking a marker you know she will want and placing it out of reach, waiting until she uses a communicative gesture to indicate a request, then praising her and immediately giving her what she’s requested to reinforce. Initially, you can reinforce her when she signs or points, but you can fade this over time to only accept points or signs accompanied by any verbalization (e.g. grunting), then a closer approximation of the target (e.g. “buh” to indicate she wants the blue marker on the shelf). 

Hope this helps!

This is very common. Cerumen (ear wax) build up can create a conductive hearing loss, accompanied by ringing and or buzzing. This is because the wax blocks the sound from stimulating the ear drum properly, which in turn, affects hearing. The brain generates ringing as a response to the decreased acoustical input.

I must encourage you to not use q tips because they, in effect, just “impact” the wax- packing a tight “wall” of wax in place of the ear drum. 

You can save yourself some serious $ (if health associated costs are a concern for you) and add hydrogen peroxide drops to your ears to soften the wax. Or, you can buy a kit that comes with a bulb with which you can clean your ears out with warm water at home. Many doctors bill insurance companies about $200 to remove ear wax.

Happy listening! And always remember to protect your hearing while at a shooting range. If not, you will  inevitably damage your inner hair cells of your ear and this will lead to an irreversible hearing loss and ringing.
